correctness.rationale: An inclusion-exclusion count enumerates every possible species-detection support for a labeled without-replacement sample. Applying the definition of expected Jaccard similarity gives a finite exact rational sum. All 29 nondecreasing positive-integer partitions through total size six were evaluated and independently checked by explicit labeled-subset pairing at 135 profile/sample cells; only abundance profile (1,5) has a downward transition, and only from two to three observations. For the analytic family (1,N-1), singleton detection is exactly Bernoulli(m/N), independently across replicates, proving the entire U-shaped phase law and its finite differences. Disjoint samples cannot both detect the singleton and give exactly 1-m/N for sample sizes >=2; domain restrictions and m=1 cases were separately checked.

originality.rationale: The inspected historical papers establish the general importance of sample-size bias and autosimilarity, but their statements do not cover the specific sharp six-individual classification together with an exact independent-versus-disjoint replicate phase law for singleton/dominant census profiles. Wolda (1981) uses logseries sampling simulations for a selection of indices rather than an exhaustive finite Jaccard classification; Chao et al. (2005) use within-replicate sampling with replacement in the directly related identical-community test. The directly relevant Cao et al. (2002) autosimilarity article could be checked only through its abstract, leaving an explicit residual bibliographic risk.

value.rationale: A natural practical baseline for ecological sampling representativeness is the similarity of replicate species inventories. Increasing effort provably need not improve this baseline monotonically, although the sample species lists themselves grow under nested coupling. The minimum possible finite population size and unique boundary profile are determined exactly. The all-size singleton/dominant family yields a persistent macroscopic U-shaped discrepancy (limiting minimum 3/4), and the independent-versus-disjoint design effect is as large as 1/4 at half census. The result changes what can legitimately be inferred from this precise index, rather than presenting an arbitrary instance of sample-size bias.
